dimension_description: Pressure is force per unit area, the intensity with which a surface is pressed. It explains why a stiletto heel dents wood while a snowshoe floats, even with the same weight. In fluids, pressure transmits uniformly and drives flow from high to low according to gradients. Every value below names a setting and condition so the number connects to daily life or specific experiments.

items.description: Between galaxies, particle densities are so low that mechanical pressure approaches zero for human purposes. Radiation fields and magnetic stresses still act, but as a pressure they are vanishingly small. Spacecraft enjoy this quiet except when hit by solar storms. The value is an order of magnitude benchmark for deep space plasma pressure.

items.description: Ultra high vacuum chambers in surface physics reach pressures near this value after long pumping and bakeout. Molecules arrive so rarely that clean crystal faces can be studied for minutes before contamination. Leak checking becomes an art at these numbers. The figure represents a good day on a research instrument.

items.description: A gentle human exhale produces only a few hundred pascals above ambient pressure, yet that is enough to move a column of air through the airway and across a flute or whistle. Respiratory therapists think in these small pressure differences when checking lung function. The number is for a calm, sustained breath rather than a forceful cough.

items.description: On the Martian surface the thin atmosphere presses at only a few hundred pascals, less than one percent of Earth sea level. Water boils at body temperature under such conditions without a suit. Weather there is driven by dust, not by dense air. The number is for a typical day at the equator.

items.description: A household vacuum cleaner creates suction by lowering pressure below room air at the nozzle. The resulting pressure difference over a modest area is what actually lifts dust and grit. Motor noise tends to obscure how small the pressure number really is compared with industrial systems. The value is a representative static suction.

items.description: Systolic blood pressure in a healthy adult corresponds to this pressure difference in arteries during a heartbeat. The body regulates it with hormones and vessel elasticity. Long term elevations increase risk for stroke and heart disease. The number is a familiar medical baseline expressed in pascals.

items.description: The water above you in a swimming pool adds pressure linearly with depth, so a few meters already feels on your ears. Lungs equalize by pushing air into sinuses, a skill every diver learns. Lifeguards know headaches often come from poor equalization rather than chlorine. The number is for a depth of two meters.

items.description: At the summit of Mount Everest the atmosphere pushes at only about a third of sea-level pressure. That thin air is why climbers need acclimatization and often supplemental oxygen. Water boils at a lower temperature there as well, changing cooking and physiology together. The number is a representative summit pressure.

items.description: Airplane cabins are pressurized to an equivalent altitude of two to three kilometers, which is lower than sea level but comfortable for most passengers. The compromise reduces structural stress and weight while keeping oxygen levels acceptable. Sensitive travelers feel mild headache or fatigue at these numbers. The value is a typical cruise cabin pressure.

items.description: At sea level on Earth, standard atmospheric pressure is about one hundred thousand pascals by definition. It sets boiling points, cooking times, and aircraft calibration. Weather systems drift a few percent above and below. The number is the canonical reference for pressure units.

Safety valves and lids are engineered against accidental opening under load. Recipes account for altitude and cooker setting. The number is for a common kitchen unit at operating pressure.

items.description: Sterilizing autoclaves run above atmospheric pressure so water can stay liquid at temperatures high enough to kill hardy microbes and spores. Laboratories and hospitals rely on this extra pressure every day, even though the absolute number is modest by engineering standards. The value is a standard operating overpressure for steam sterilization.

items.description: A typical can of carbonated soda holds an overpressure relative to air that keeps bubbles dissolved. Warming the can raises this pressure and makes foaming more likely on opening. Manufacturers choose levels to balance fizz and safety. The value is for a chilled sealed can.

items.description: A passenger car tire is inflated to a few bars over atmospheric pressure to balance grip, wear, and comfort. Underinflation wastes fuel and overheats sidewalls, while overinflation reduces contact patch. Temperature changes during driving shift the number significantly. The value is for a warm tire after highway travel.

items.description: A hyperbaric chamber used for diving medicine runs at a few atmospheres to treat decompression sickness. Breathing pure oxygen at these pressures accelerates nitrogen washout. Operators monitor for oxygen toxicity risks. The value is a representative treatment pressure.

items.description: Aerosol cans store propellant at several bars so the spray stays strong until the container is nearly empty. Warming the can raises internal pressure, which is why safety labels warn against heat and fire. The number is typical for room-temperature consumer spray cans. It is an overpressure relative to ambient conditions.

items.description: Road bicycles run far above car-tire pressure because their contact patches are small and rolling resistance matters. Riders trade comfort against pinch-flat resistance and speed by adjusting within this range. A floor pump gauge makes the number feel ordinary even though it is several atmospheres. The value is for a narrow road tire.

That is why corks eject so energetically when restraint is removed. Temperature matters strongly because dissolved gas and headspace both respond to warming. The number is a common room-temperature bottle pressure.

That pressure is high enough to extract oils and emulsify crema in seconds rather than minutes. Home machines advertise it prominently because the number is part of the drink’s identity. The value is the classic brewing pressure target.

Steel hulls and polymer seals are sized with generous safety margins. Breathing gas composition must change to avoid nitrogen narcosis. The value is a round figure for this depth.

Metals soften and electronics require special cooling even before the heat is considered. Probes survive only hours with heroic engineering. The value is for the mean surface under cloud cover.

That is a hundred times sea-level atmospheric pressure pressing on every viewport, seal, and instrument housing. Deep-ocean vehicles live or die by whether they keep this number outside. The value is a round figure for 1000 meters depth.

items.description: Industrial hydraulic systems routinely operate at tens to hundreds of bars to move heavy loads precisely. Hoses and fittings are rated well above working pressure to prevent catastrophic sprays. Small leaks feel deceptively gentle but can inject fluid into skin. The number is a mid range for shop presses and lifts.

The value is a round-number benchmark for abyssal water.

It is a standard automotive storage pressure.

Only specialized research vessels and adapted organisms operate here. Material imperfections become critical under such loads. The number gives the scale at the deepest natural point on Earth.

That helps engines burn more cleanly and precisely, but it also makes leaks medically dangerous because fuel can penetrate skin. The number shows how far everyday automotive hardware reaches into high-pressure engineering. This value is a modern common-rail scale.

The value is a representative cutting-head pressure.

This pressure and temperature together power the geodynamo. The number is a standard estimate for the center.

units.description: The pascal is the SI pressure unit equal to one newton per square meter of area. It connects force and geometry directly for analysis. Using pascals allows pressures in gases, liquids, and solids to be compared consistently. All item values are recorded in pascals before conversion.
units.name: pascals

units.description: Atmospheres are tied to mean sea level air pressure on Earth and remain convenient for diving and meteorology. They give an intuitive sense of how many Earth atmospheres a device or body experiences. Converting to pascals is linear by definition. Values here use the conventional standard atmosphere.
units.name: atmospheres

units.description: Pounds per square inch is the imperial unit used for tires, hydraulics, and tools in North America. Gauges on cars and compressors often display psi prominently. Conversions help align those readings with SI calculations. The factor assumes exact definitions of pound and inch.
units.name: pounds per square inch

units.description: The bar equals one hundred thousand pascals and is common in engineering because round numbers are convenient. Weather maps and compressor ratings often use bars. It is not an SI unit but is compatible by a simple factor. We include it to make comparisons readable.
units.name: bars

units.description: Torr measures pressure based on mercury columns, with one torr equal to one seven hundred sixtieth of an atmosphere. Vacuum technology still uses it because old gauges and tables were calibrated this way. Modern sensors output pascals but many labs speak in torr out of habit. The conversion factor links the two worlds cleanly.
units.name: torr

units.description: Kilopascals are common in weather, tires, and engineering contexts.
units.name: kilopascals

units.description: Megapascals are useful for high-pressure engineering and materials.
units.name: megapascals
